analysis.one_liner: Requires all US gasoline to contain 10 percent ethanol and all diesel 5 percent biodiesel after 2010.
analysis.headline: The ethanol and biodiesel blend mandate never received a committee vote and died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten the Clean Air Act to force a nationwide fuel blend: after December 31, 2010, every gallon of gasoline sold in the contiguous United States would have to contain at least 10 percent ethanol, and every gallon of diesel at least 5 percent biodiesel. The sponsor's stated aims were reducing dependence on imported oil, raising farm income, and cutting certain tailpipe emissions. The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Energy and Air Quality subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: The clearest winners would be corn growers, ethanol producers, soybean growers, and biodiesel producers: a federal mandate that every gallon of gasoline and diesel contain their product creates a guaranteed, permanent market regardless of demand or price. The bill's findings also claim benefits for truckers and farmers facing high fuel bills through reduced reliance on imported oil, and for people with respiratory ailments through claimed emission reductions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Corn and soybean growers, ethanol and biodiesel makers

how_it_helps.text: After 2010, every gallon of gasoline sold in the contiguous United States would have to contain at least 10 percent ethanol, and every gallon of diesel at least 5 percent biodiesel, displacing a corresponding share of petroleum fuel and imported oil.

The bill's findings argue that a sustained market of 100 million gallons of biodiesel alone would add $170 million a year to farm income, and that ethanol blending cuts tailpipe carbon monoxide up to 30 percent and smog-forming emissions.
The findings tie the mandate to energy security, citing the vulnerability created by heavy reliance on imported petroleum and the 2005 price of about $55 per barrel.

analysis.who_pays: Drivers and fuel buyers would bear any added blending cost and a small mileage penalty, since ethanol carries less energy per gallon than gasoline. Oil refiners and petroleum importers would lose roughly 10 percent of the gasoline market and 5 percent of the diesel market to mandated biofuels. Regions without nearby ethanol or biodiesel supply would face higher logistics costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Drivers at the pump; oil refiners

drawbacks.text: The mandate applied to every gallon of gasoline and diesel sold in the contiguous United States after 2010, with no waiver or regional flexibility, so areas far from ethanol or biodiesel production would have had to bear the cost of shipping biofuels in.

Ethanol contains roughly one-third less energy per gallon than gasoline, so a 10 percent blend slightly reduces miles per gallon, and any added blending costs would likely be passed on to drivers at the pump.

The bill's own findings credit grain ethanol with cutting greenhouse gas emissions 35 to 46 percent versus gasoline, but independent research has since questioned whether corn ethanol delivers a meaningful net climate benefit once farming, fertilizer, and processing are counted.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential gains were real but modest: somewhat less dependence on imported oil and somewhat higher farm income, at the cost of a small fuel-economy penalty for every driver, a rigid nationwide requirement with no regional flexibility or waiver, and climate benefits that independent research has seriously questioned for grain ethanol. The bill also contained no cost cap or safety valve, so any supply squeeze would have fallen directly on pump prices. A designed-more-carefully mandate might have netted a benefit; this version tilted toward guaranteeing a market for the biofuel industry.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Energy and Air Quality subcommittee, which never acted on it before the Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Representative Marcy Kaptur introduced the bill on March 17, 2005, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
Five days later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality, where it sat with no hearings, markup, or floor vote for the rest of the Congress.
The only further activity was a sponsor's introductory remarks printed in the Congressional Record on April 26, 2006, more than a year after introduction.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without action, oil refiners and fuel blenders never had to meet the blend mandate. Corn farmers and ethanol producers gained nothing from this bill, though Congress enacted a separate, less sweeping renewable fuel requirement later in 2005.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil refiners and blenders, spared the mandate

sides.party_line_note: Only Democrats sponsored or cosponsored the bill, and no vote was ever taken, so the partisan shape of support and opposition is unknown from the record.

industries.industry: Corn ethanol producers and corn farmers
industries.note: A 10 percent blend requirement would guarantee a market for ethanol in every gallon of gasoline sold nationwide after 2010, a far larger and more certain commitment than the voluntary E-85 market the bill describes (only 400 of 187,000 stations sold E-85). That locked-in demand mainly benefits ethanol plants and corn growers.

The 5 percent diesel mandate would create a guaranteed nationwide market for biodiesel, which the bill notes was only 25 million gallons in 2003. Drivers would bear any blending cost and the fuel-economy penalty of biodiesel blends.

The mandate would displace roughly 10 percent of gasoline volume and 5 percent of diesel with biofuels, cutting demand for petroleum products and imports. Refiners and blenders would also handle the logistics of blending nationwide.
